transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jared Patel (Redwood SE), Ayesha Rahman (CinderPoint Head Platform), Liam O'Connor (SRE Lead), Rafael Mora (CTO)

Summary:
CinderPoint is evaluating Redwood for a hybrid deployment: hosted for lower-tier traffic, Dedicated pools for latency-sensitive tenants, and a Private VPC option for regulated clients. Primary concerns are SLO guarantees for <200ms p95 on high-priority tenants, fallback behavior during regional outages, how billing interacts with fallback (tokens + burst capacity), and audit/KMS integration for Private. Team wants an ops-handoff playbook and contractual SLA language that covers partial degradation scenarios.

Topics covered:
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit for multi-tenant regulatory constraints
- Multi-region routing and automatic model-variant fallback
- Circuit breaker behavior and grace periods during scale events
- Latency SLAs and how to measure / penalize partial degradation
- Benchmarking plan and pilot scope

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros?
[00:08] Ayesha (CinderPoint): hi, Ayesha here, i run platform and infra, we're primarily evaluating the resiliency story.
[00:13] Liam (CinderPoint): Liam, SRE lead, i'll drive the benchmarks and runbooks on our side.
[00:18] Rafael (CinderPoint): Rafael, CTO, interested in contractual SLAs and data residency for some customers.
[00:23] Maya: perfect. Jared from my team is the systems lead, he'll do the technical deep-dive — Jared?
[00:28] Jared (Redwood SE): yea hi all, quick note i'm gonna cover routing/fallbacks and practical impact on latency. bear with me if i stumble on product names i sometimes say Redwood Dedicate or Redwood Private — same product family.
[00:40] Ayesha: yeah we saw the doc you shared, curious about the "fallback tiers" you mentioned — specifically how traffic is rerouted if a region hits an outage but Dedicated pool in another region is healthy.
[00:50] Jared: good question. we do policy-based routing: you can set prefer-region rules, with automatic failover to a secondary region. important nuance — failover has two axes: routing (instant redirect at the api/gateway) and cold-starts on Dedicated pools if capacity isn't pre-warmed. so for strict <200ms p95 tenants you'd want either multi-region warm pools or Hosted with geo-redundant capacity and a fallback model variant that's quantized for lower-latency.
[01:18] Liam: when you say "warm pools" what are realistic incur costs and warm-up times?
[01:22] Jared: warm pools are reserved, idle-ready GPUs — instant routing. cost is the reserved capacity charge (monthly or commit), we gave an example in the deck but to be clear: warm pools remove autoscaler cold starts. warm-up for new model variants can be 30s-2m if not pre-cached; KV cache priming for common prefixes can add some tens of ms per token if miss rates are high.
[01:39] Rafael: so if regionA fails and we failover to regionB, is there an SLA credit if latency goes from 120ms to 400ms? how is that contractualized?
[01:48] Maya: historically we tier SLAs. for hard outages we have availability SLAs (percent uptime). partial degradation clauses are trickier — we propose measured SLOs per route/model (p95 latency, error budget). in contract we can define a golden path: if p95 exceeds threshold for X mins we trigger remediation and credits. i'll flag legal about specific language but we can propose a clause for "degraded operation" that is different from total outage.
[02:15] Ayesha: hmm we have customers that require a hard p95 <200ms, can't have occasional 400ms spikes during failover. is the only option Dedicated multi-region with warm pools?
[02:24] Jared: essentially yes if you need hard guarantees. you can also do hybrid: host primary on Dedicated single-region with warm secondary region for the high-tier tenants, and for lower-tier traffic let Hosted absorb. also model-variant fallback: if our full model is heavy we can serve a smaller quantized variant during failover which tends to reduce latency but might change output characteristics.
[02:45] Liam: i'm worried about output regressions during fallback. our product requires fairly consistent responses or a rollback path.
[02:51] Jared: agreed — part of the pilot should include quality gating and eval prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can hook into your evals to monitor regressions and alert. also we recommend canary traffic split: 95/5 to fallback first, run A/B checks, then ramp.
[03:06] Ayesha: how does billing work when traffic hits Hosted fallback? do we get double-billed or any weird spikes?
[03:12] Maya: billing is per-token + reserved capacity charges. if you configure automatic failover to Hosted, tokens are billed against Hosted pricing for those requests; Reserved Dedicated pools still bill as committed. we can model blended costs for you — that will be in Jared's throughput/cost deck.
[03:29] Rafael: okay we need cost predictability for procurement. also we need KMS/HSM integration and audit logs retained for 12 months for regulated customers. how does Private fit?
[03:38] Maya: Redwood Private is a customer-managed VPC option — we deploy a private control plane and inference nodes in your VPC or on-prem. KMS plug-ins for AWS KMS or customer HSM are supported; audit logs can ship to your S3/logging stack. there is an ops overhead for initial setup and you'll get platform fees.
[03:54] Liam: on the private side, during a region-level networking flap, do we still get cross-region fallback? in our security posture cross-region data movement is restricted.
[04:01] Jared: by default Private keeps data in customer network. cross-region fallback for Private is possible but would require you to allow peering / replication policies. if cross-region is blocked we can still fallback to a local lighter-weight model or degrade feature set (e.g., disable embeddings, or limit max tokens) to preserve latency inside region. that's a policy you configure per-tenant/route.
[04:25] Ayesha: what about circuit breakers — how aggressive are they and can we tune them per-route?
[04:29] Jared: yes per-route circuit breakers. you can set error rate thresholds, token exhaustion thresholds and dynamically throttle. we offer graceful degradation policies: serve cached responses, short cached embeddings, or return synthetic "service degraded" responses with a structured fallback payload so your app knows it's a fallback.
[04:49] Rafael: can we see a sample "degraded response" payload so product can detect it?
[04:52] Jared: yes we'll include examples — usually a top-level field like "redwood_fallback": true plus metadata about reason and source model. note the fallback model id might differ and you'll want to map acceptance criteria.
[05:05] Liam: benchmarks — we're going to run p95 and p99 across peak hour traffic with both normal and simulated region loss. we need a plan.
[05:11] Maya: plan: 1) Redwood shares a benchmark harness and scripts, 2) CinderPoint provides traffic profile and tenants, 3) joint run with SREs where Redwood runs a warm Dedicated pool and then triggers failover. we should do an initial smoke test then the full stress test.
[05:25] Ayesha: timeline? procurement needs numbers in ~2 weeks.
[05:28] Maya: we can deliver a draft cost and SLA proposal in five business days if you share traffic numbers by Friday. Jared?
[05:35] Jared: yes, i'll model batch sizes, expected token rates, KV cache hit assumptions. i'll include an optimistic and conservative scenario. also, a note on autoscaling: if you rely on burst autoscale without reserved capacity you should expect cold starts which can spike latency for a minute or two while kernels warm.
[05:53] Liam: on cold starts, any mitigation? pre-warming hooks?
[05:56] Jared: you can attach pre-warm policies or schedule warm windows during peaks. we also have prefilling for KV caches via synthetic warm requests, which reduces first-requests misses.
[06:08] Ayesha: Security checklist: SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit retention, KMS, penetration test support, legal — do you support SOC2 and ISO reports for Private?
[06:18] Maya: yes SOC2 type II and ISO summaries available; we'll include them in the security pack. Private also supports customer-provided KMS and audit sinks. we'll note the pen-test scoping — some customers run a third-party pentest after deployment.
[06:30] Rafael: one contract question — will Redwood accept SLA credits tied to partial degradation or only total downtime?
[06:36] Maya: we can propose a layered SLA. full outage (control plane or node unavailability) triggers classic uptime credits. partial degradation (consistent p95 breach for a defined window) can map to a separate credit schedule, but legal needs to align on measurable metrics and exclusion sections (e.g., customer misconfig, network blackholes). i'll coordinate legal on sample language.
[07:00] Liam: are there latency objectives you can guarantee for Hosted?
[07:04] Jared: Hosted has regionally documented latency profiles; best-effort SLAs focus on availability. for hard p95 latency guarantees, Dedicated or Private reserved capacity is the path. Hosted is low-friction but less deterministic under wide spikes.
[07:18] Ayesha: we have ~30 tenants that need the strict SLA. can we do a mix where those 30 are Dedicated and others are Hosted?
[07:23] Maya: absolutely — that's a typical setup. you configure per-tenant routing rules and RBAC ensures only those tenants hit Dedicated.
[07:32] Rafael: regarding fallback: what about model fidelity drift — logs and evals are retained so we can show customers the delta?
[07:38] Jared: yes, Redwood Optimize ties evals to rollouts. we can snapshot outputs before/after fallback and generate regression stats. we'll include that in the pilot scope.
[07:48] Ayesha: are there any limits on number of model variants or custom quantized builds for Dedicated?
[07:53] Jared: you can pin model versions; for custom quantized builds there are some operational steps. we support up to N custom variants per commit in Dedicated; i'll specify limits in my follow-up. generally it's fine but build time and validation increase the turnaround.
[08:07] Maya: ok let's surface a short ops-handoff checklist — what does CinderPoint need to have to take on runbook?
[08:12] Liam: runbook needs: traffic profiles, tenant list, incident playbooks, SSH/K8s access patterns, logging endpoints, and a runbook owner.
[08:20] Maya: we'll produce a runbook template and example playbooks for failover, plus a vendor contact tree for escalations.
[08:27] Rafael: last bit, procurement: they will ask for a pilot term and an escape clause if SLAs are not met.
[08:33] Maya: that's normal. we'll offer a 3-month pilot with clear acceptance criteria: p95 target, regression threshold on eval prompts, and handoff readiness. if acceptance fails, you can terminate without conversion.
[08:44] Ayesha: sounds good.
[08:46] Maya: ok quick recap and next steps?
[08:49] Maya: recap: 1) Redwood to send security pack (SOC2/ISO, KMS notes) 2) Jared to deliver cost/throughput scenarios and fallback latency estimates 3) CinderPoint to send traffic profiles and priority tenant list by Friday 4) schedule benchmark week of Apr 19.
[09:07] Ayesha: we'll get the traffic export and list sent.
[09:10] Liam: i'll coordinate SRE for the bench.
[09:13] Rafael: legal will review proposed SLA language.
[09:15] Maya: perfect. thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with calendar invites.

Action items (recap):
- Maya: security pack + sample SLA language (due 2027-04-14)
- Jared: cost/throughput model + fallback latency scenarios (due 2027-04-16)
- CinderPoint (Ayesha): traffic profiles + priority tenant list (due 2027-04-15)

End of transcript.
